claims.text: The dynamic mechanical response of solidified Co-free FeNiCrMn is governed by temperature- and strain-rate-dependent activation of dislocation-based plasticity.
Rapid solidification of FeNiCrMn produces a fine-grained microstructure containing a high density of grain boundaries and dislocation networks.
Fine grains and associated grain boundaries and dislocation networks govern dislocation and twin-interface nucleation and mobility in FeNiCrMn.
At lower temperatures and/or higher strain rates, limited thermal activation restricts dislocation mobility in FeNiCrMn.
Restricted dislocation mobility at lower temperatures and/or higher strain rates increases the propensity for deformation twinning.
The low-temperature or high-strain-rate regime increases strength while reducing ductility.
At higher temperatures and/or lower strain rates, dislocation climb and cross-slip become enhanced in FeNiCrMn.
Enhanced climb and cross-slip lower the activation barrier for slip.
Easier slip at higher temperatures and/or lower strain rates reduces yield strength and improves ductility.
Yield strength will systematically increase as temperature decreases or strain rate increases.
Ductility will systematically decrease as temperature decreases or strain rate increases.
Low-temperature and high-strain-rate deformation will produce a greater prevalence of deformation twins than elevated-temperature deformation.
Low-temperature and high-strain-rate deformation will produce higher dislocation density than elevated-temperature deformation.
Elevated-temperature deformation will produce more homogeneously distributed dislocations.
Room-temperature quasi-static tests on solidified FeNiCrMn have established a balance of strength and ductility.

The proposed mechanism is limited to rapidly solidified, fine-grained material below melting and phase-transformation temperatures and outside regimes dominated by brittle fracture or extrinsic failure.
The transition temperature and strain rate separating twinning-dominated and slip-dominated regimes are not yet quantitatively known.
Incipient phase transformation may contribute to the observed dynamic response.
